items.title: Nature & Scope of Science, Technology and Innovation
items.body:
## Three distinct ideas

- **Science** = the systematic pursuit of **knowledge about the natural world** through observation, experiment and reasoning.
- **Technology** = the **application of scientific knowledge** to solve practical problems and create tools, processes and products.
- **Innovation** = the **successful introduction** of a new or improved product, process or service into **use or the market** (invention + adoption/value). Invention alone is not innovation.

## Relevance to daily life

- S&T underpins **health (vaccines, diagnostics), agriculture (HYV seeds, weather forecasts), communication (UPI, mobile), transport, energy and disaster warning**.
- **Science-Technology-Innovation (STI)** is treated as an engine of economic growth and self-reliance (**Atmanirbhar Bharat**), and of achieving the SDGs.

## Scientific temper

- **Article 51A(h)** makes it a **Fundamental Duty** of every citizen to develop the **scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform** (inserted by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**).
- India is one of the few countries to constitutionally mention scientific temper — a phrase popularised by Nehru.
keyPoints: Science = knowledge of the natural world; Technology = applying that knowledge; Innovation = successful real-world use of a new/improved product or process.
Invention is not the same as innovation — innovation requires adoption/value.
Article 51A(h) makes developing scientific temper, humanism and spirit of inquiry a Fundamental Duty.
Fundamental Duties (incl. 51A(h)) were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
STI drives Atmanirbhar Bharat and everyday services like health, agriculture and UPI.
items.mnemonic: Know it (Science) -> Build it (Technology) -> Use it widely (Innovation).
items.source: DST STI policy framework; Constitution of India Article 51A(h)

items.title: Evolution of India's S&T Policy (1958 to draft 2020)
items.body:
## Five policy milestones

India has adopted **four** S&T policies, with a **fifth in draft**:

| Policy | Year | Era | Thrust |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scientific Policy Resolution (SPR) | 1958 | Nehru | Cultivate science & scientific temper; benefits of science for the people |
| Technology Policy Statement (TPS) | 1983 | Indira Gandhi | **Technological self-reliance**; indigenous capability |
| Science & Technology Policy (STP) | 2003 | Vajpayee | Integrate S&T; raise investment; innovation & equity |
| Science, Technology & Innovation Policy (STIP) | 2013 | Manmohan Singh | 'STI **for the People**'; top-5 scientific power; **2% GERD** goal |
| Draft STIP | 2020 | — | **Fifth** policy; **decentralised, bottom-up**; still a draft, not notified |

## Key shifts

- The word **'Innovation'** entered the policy title only in **2013**.
- **STIP 2020** was drafted by the **Office of the PSA + DST** through a wide consultative process; as of 2026 it is **not yet formally adopted**.
- The **2% GERD target** (STIP 2013) remains unmet — actual spend is about **0.64% of GDP**.
keyPoints: Four adopted S&T policies: SPR 1958, TPS 1983, STP 2003, STIP 2013; STIP 2020 is a draft.
SPR 1958 (Nehru) stressed scientific temper; TPS 1983 stressed technological self-reliance.
'Innovation' entered the policy title only with STIP 2013.
STIP 2013 aimed to put India among the top 5 scientific powers and raise GERD to 2% of GDP.
Draft STIP 2020 (PSA + DST) is decentralised/bottom-up and not yet notified.
items.mnemonic: Policy order 'S-T-S-S' years 58-83-03-13 (SPR, TPS, STP, STIP).
items.source: DST (dst.gov.in) — evolution of S&T policy; draft STIP 2020

items.title: Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF), 2023
items.body:
## What it is

- Set up under the **Anusandhan National Research Foundation Act, 2023** as the **apex body** to fund, coordinate and promote research across **natural sciences, technology, agriculture, health and allied fields**.
- It **subsumed the Science and Engineering Research Board (SERB)** (est. 2008).

## Funding & governance

- Envisaged outlay of about **Rs 50,000 crore over 2023-28**; a **large share (about Rs 36,000 crore) is expected from non-government sources** — industry and philanthropy — a deliberate push for **private funding** of research.
- **Governing Board** is headed by the **Prime Minister** as ex-officio President; the Union Ministers of Science & Technology and Education are Vice-Presidents.
- Aligns with the **National Education Policy 2020** goal of a research-driven ecosystem; PM Modi chaired the **first Governing Board meeting in September 2024**.
keyPoints: ANRF was created under the ANRF Act, 2023 and replaced the SERB (2008).
It is the apex body funding research in natural sciences, technology, agriculture and health.
Outlay about Rs 50,000 crore over 2023-28, with about Rs 36,000 crore expected from private/non-government sources.
The Prime Minister is ex-officio President of its Governing Board.
It advances the NEP 2020 vision of a research-led ecosystem; first Board meeting held Sept 2024.
items.source: Anusandhan National Research Foundation Act, 2023; PIB

items.title: Key S&T Institutions & Administrative Structure
items.body:
## Ministry of Science and Technology

Has **three departments**:

| Department | Year | Mandate |
|---|---|---|
| **DST** | 1971 | Promote & coordinate S&T; runs many schemes/missions |
| **DBT** | 1986 | Biotechnology R&D and applications |
| **DSIR** | — | Industrial research; **parent of CSIR** |

## Major research organisations

- **CSIR** (1942, under DSIR) — a network of about **37 laboratories** (e.g., NPL, NCL, CCMB & IICT in Hyderabad); one of the world's largest publicly funded R&D bodies.
- **DAE** (1954) — works **directly under the Prime Minister**; associated with **Homi J. Bhabha**; units include **BARC, IGCAR, NPCIL**.
- Other apex bodies: **ICMR** (medical), **ICAR** (agriculture), **DRDO** (defence), **ISRO** (space, under Dept of Space).

## Advisory architecture

- **Principal Scientific Adviser (PSA)** advises the government on S&T; chairs the **PM's Science, Technology and Innovation Advisory Council (PM-STIAC)**.
- Premier institutes: **IISc Bengaluru, TIFR, IITs, IISERs**.
keyPoints: Ministry of Science & Technology has three departments: DST (1971), DBT (1986) and DSIR.
CSIR (1942) works under DSIR and runs about 37 laboratories.
DAE (1954) functions directly under the PM and is linked to Homi J. Bhabha (BARC, IGCAR, NPCIL).
ICMR (medical), ICAR (agriculture), DRDO (defence) and ISRO (space) are other apex S&T bodies.
The PSA advises the government and chairs PM-STIAC; DST is headed by its Secretary, not the PSA.
items.mnemonic: Ministry's three D's = DST, DBT, DSIR (DAE is separate, under the PM).

items.title: Mission-Mode S&T Initiatives
items.body:
## Flagship missions

| Mission | Year | Outlay / scale | Focus |
|---|---|---|---|
| **National Quantum Mission** | 2023 | **Rs 6003.65 cr** (2023-24 to 2030-31) | Quantum computing, communication, sensing, materials (4 hubs) |
| **National Supercomputing Mission** | 2015 | — | Indigenous **PARAM** supercomputers (e.g., PARAM Rudra) via C-DAC |
| **NM-ICPS** | 2018 | about Rs 3,660 cr | Cyber-Physical Systems; **25 Technology Innovation Hubs** |
| **RDI Scheme** | 2025 | about **Rs 1 lakh crore** corpus | Long-tenure, low-cost finance for **private-sector R&D** in sunrise/strategic sectors |

## Why mission-mode

- These target **deep-tech** and strategic autonomy, and try to **crowd in private investment** to lift India's low GERD.
- The **RDI Scheme (2025)** complements — does not replace — the **ANRF**, addressing the weak private-sector share in R&D funding.
keyPoints: National Quantum Mission (2023): Rs 6003.65 crore, 2023-24 to 2030-31, four thematic hubs.
National Supercomputing Mission delivers indigenous PARAM supercomputers via C-DAC.
NM-ICPS (2018) focuses on Cyber-Physical Systems and set up 25 Technology Innovation Hubs.
RDI Scheme (2025): about Rs 1 lakh crore corpus to finance private-sector R&D in sunrise sectors.
RDI Scheme complements ANRF; both aim to raise India's low GERD.
items.source: PIB — National Quantum Mission, RDI Scheme; DST — NSM, NM-ICPS

items.title: R&D Spend, Innovation Ranking & Recent Initiatives
items.body:
## R&D spending (GERD)

- India's **Gross Expenditure on R&D (GERD)** is about **0.64% of GDP** — far below the STIP 2013 target of **2%** and below peers (China about 2.4%, USA/Israel/Korea higher).
- A distinctive feature: the **government funds the bulk of R&D**, while the **private-sector share is low** — the gap the ANRF and RDI Scheme aim to close.

## Global Innovation Index (GII)

- Published annually by the **World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO)**.
- India ranked **39th in GII 2024** and **38th in GII 2025**, and consistently **tops the lower-middle-income group** and the Central & Southern Asia region.

## Recent enabling initiatives (2024-25)

- **One Nation One Subscription (ONOS)** — operational **1 January 2025**; centrally funded access to thousands of e-journals via the **INFLIBNET Centre (UGC)** (about Rs 6,000 cr for 2025-27).
- **Vigyan Dhara** — a unified DST central-sector scheme (2024) **merging three umbrella schemes** (outlay about Rs 10,579.84 cr for 2021-26).
keyPoints: India's GERD is about 0.64% of GDP, well short of the 2% aspiration.
Government funds most R&D in India; the private-sector share is comparatively low.
The Global Innovation Index is published by WIPO; India was 39th (2024) and 38th (2025).
India tops the lower-middle-income group in the GII.
ONOS (operational 1 Jan 2025, via INFLIBNET/UGC) and Vigyan Dhara (2024 DST scheme merger) are recent enablers.
items.source: DST R&D Statistics; WIPO GII 2024/2025; PIB — ONOS, Vigyan Dhara

items.title: Science & Technology Institutions in Andhra Pradesh
items.body:
## Space & atmospheric science

- **Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR), Sriharikota** — ISRO's **primary spaceport** (launch complex for PSLV/GSLV/LVM3), on an island in Tirupati district.
- **National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL), Gadanki** — an **autonomous DST** institute near Tirupati for atmospheric and radar science.

## Premier education & research (post-2014)

| Institution | Location (AP) |
|---|---|
| **IIT Tirupati** (3rd-gen IIT) | Yerpedu, Tirupati |
| **IISER Tirupati** | Tirupati |
| **NIT Andhra Pradesh** (est. 2015) | Tadepalligudem (West Godavari) |
| **IIPE** (Petroleum & Energy) | Visakhapatnam |
| **AIIMS** | Mangalagiri (near Guntur) |

## Innovation ecosystem

- **Amaravati Quantum Valley** — a planned **quantum computing hub** in the capital region, intended to attract industry partners (IBM, TCS, L&T) and investment.
- **Careful — NOT in AP:** national labs at **Hyderabad** — **CCMB, IICT, NGRI** — remained in **Telangana** after the 2014 bifurcation.
keyPoints: SDSC-SHAR (Sriharikota) is ISRO's primary spaceport; NARL is at Gadanki near Tirupati.
Tirupati hosts both an IIT (Yerpedu) and an IISER.
NIT Andhra Pradesh is at Tadepalligudem; IIPE is at Visakhapatnam; AIIMS is at Mangalagiri.
Amaravati Quantum Valley is a planned quantum-computing hub in AP's capital region.
CCMB, IICT and NGRI are in Hyderabad (Telangana), NOT Andhra Pradesh.
items.mnemonic: AP tech map: Sriharikota (space), Tirupati (IIT+IISER+NARL), Vizag (IIPE), Tadepalligudem (NIT), Mangalagiri (AIIMS), Amaravati (Quantum).
items.source: ISRO SDSC-SHAR; NARL; IIT Tirupati; IISER Tirupati; NIT AP; IIPE; AIIMS Mangalagiri; Govt of AP (Amaravati Quantum Valley)
